question: What can an orchestra reveal before a character sings?
intro: Before Violetta’s party begins, Verdi contrasts exposed high strings with a broader melody that returns later in the opera. How does the prelude change your expectations before any singer appears?

sections.label: Melody with decoration
sections.mNote: cantabile moves to lower strings beneath quick violin decoration

cues.title: The exposed opening
cues.text: The score opens with quiet, divided high strings rather than the weight of the full orchestra. Compare that exposed texture with the broader melody later in the prelude; it can suggest a vulnerability quite unlike the party scene that follows.
cues.evidence: The instrumentation comes from the score; the dramatic reading is an interpretation, not something established by the noisy transfer’s pitch estimates.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Venice, March 1853
cues.text: La traviata was first performed at La Fenice on 6 March 1853, with a libretto by Francesco Maria Piave. Its central figure, Violetta, is a Parisian courtesan whose relationship with Alfredo is constrained by illness and social respectability.
cues.evidence: English National Opera’s introduction gives the premiere details, authorship and central dramatic situation.

cues.title: A swell within the introduction
cues.text: The introductory span grows stronger and then withdraws before the broader melody. Follow the whole rise and release: the opening has its own phrase shape, rather than merely filling time before a singer enters.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 1:05–1:10 and falls substantially towards 1:20.

cues.title: A contemporary French source
cues.text: Piave adapted Alexandre Dumas fils’s La Dame aux camélias, whose heroine Marguerite Gautier became Violetta. The novel appeared in 1848 and Dumas’s stage adaptation opened in Paris in 1852, only a year before the opera.
cues.evidence: Julie Anselmini’s BnF account dates the novel and play and traces the adaptation into Verdi’s opera.

cues.title: A melody beneath decoration
cues.text: In the decorated passage, listen through the lighter upper activity to the longer melody underneath. That melody is associated with Violetta’s Act II plea “Amami, Alfredo” — “Love me, Alfredo”; here it is an orchestral line, not a sung text.
cues.evidence: The score establishes the melodic connection; the audio change around 2:10 only helps locate the decorated span approximately.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A household outside marriage
cues.text: When Verdi composed La traviata, he was living at Sant’Agata with the retired soprano Giuseppina Strepponi. They moved there in 1851 and married in 1859; these circumstances do not by themselves make the opera autobiographical.
cues.evidence: Dino Rizzo’s Treccani biography records the move to Sant’Agata and the marriage date.

cues.title: The quiet closing span
cues.text: The prelude’s decorated writing recedes towards a quiet close. Listen through the diminishing sound rather than waiting for a brilliant final flourish: the party belongs to the stage scene after the prelude.
cues.evidence: Relative level remains low across 3:20–3:35 and falls further in the final window, which has no detected new attacks.

transitions.title: A regular bass gives the melody support
transitions.how: The chromatic high-string introduction broadens and diminishes before the cantabile establishes a firmer E-major setting. Verdi brings the melody into a fuller register and gives it regularly articulated bass and chordal support, replacing the opening’s exposed, sustained sonorities. The new line is the melody associated later with “Amami, Alfredo”, not simply the high opening figure made louder. The underlying accompaniment makes its long notes possible: the bass can keep the phrase moving while the tune holds, leans and releases.
transitions.evidence: The cantabile boundary is 1:25, close to the measured change at 1:28. Analysis shows the introductory swell at 1:05–1:10, withdrawal by 1:20 and renewed weight at 1:25–1:30. The score supplies the allargando and diminuendo, E-major cantabile and newly regular accompaniment. A public Schirmer reduction shows the join on printed p. 1: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/64/IMSLP392071-PMLP16223-TraviataVSschIEco.pdf. The transfer’s pitch estimates are not used to name chords.

transitions.title: The tune moves below the violin decoration
transitions.how: A quieter linking passage gives the melody to the lower strings, with clarinet and bassoon support, while the violins begin light, quick decoration above it. The E-major melodic argument continues: Verdi changes the distribution of attention rather than requiring a new key or a new principal tune. The bass still supports the cantabile’s longer phrases, but the upper notes now articulate a much smaller rhythmic scale. Follow the lower song through the join; the most active line is no longer the melody.
transitions.evidence: The decorated-melody boundary is 2:10, the strongest measured change. The score supplies the cello link and the lower melodic doubling beneath violin figures; these assignments are labelled in the Schirmer reduction on printed p. 1. The report locates the textural region but cannot identify those instruments in the noisy mono transfer. No literal audio-match relation is available.

transitions.title: The decoration contracts around the final tonic
transitions.how: The decorated paragraph loses both weight and continuity. Shorter upper-string gestures replace the sustained sweep of the earlier line, while the bass brings the harmony back to E major through its B dominant. Verdi lets the tonic settle quietly rather than crowning it with a brilliant orchestral flourish. The distinction between melody and ornament gradually gives way to isolated closing gestures and their resonance. This is the prelude’s own cadence; the stage party that follows is not included in this recording.
transitions.evidence: The quiet-close boundary is 3:18, a measured change before the low-level span at 3:20–3:35 and terminal decay. The score supplies the E-major cadential destination and thinning string texture. Exact chord attacks and the final release have not been aligned; the transfer’s persistent pitch contamination is not treated as harmonic evidence.

source.title: Verdi, La traviata, full score (Milan: G. Ricordi, 1914, plate 113958; Dover reprint)
source.locator: No. 1, Preludio, printed pp. 1–6; bars placed between the file’s section times

timeline.note: Eight solo violins, divided, in the highest register; nothing else sounds.
Violas and cellos enter; a solo clarinet and horn join the violins.
Cantabile in E major: violins sing over soft repeated wind notes and a plucked bass.
The tune moves to violas and cellos, supported by clarinet and bassoon, as the violins decorate.
A solo horn joins; the clarinet sings above the divided violins.
The decoration thickens: violin trills and figures with short wind phrases over the cellos.
Quiet close: allargando, diminuendo, morendo; the whole ensemble dying away.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a change of vocal phrase, bass note or ensemble balance alter the relations between people on stage.
facts: Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto; private study with Vincenzo Lavigna in Milan after rejection by the Conservatoire
La Scala, Milan · La Fenice, Venice · Paris Opéra · theatres in Naples, Rome, St Petersburg and Cairo
Francesco Maria Piave, Salvadore Cammarano and Arrigo Boito among his principal librettists
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred pieces, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Verdi was born in Le Roncole, near Busseto, where his parents kept an inn and shop. He learnt the organ locally and studied with Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto. The merchant and amateur musician Antonio Barezzi helped finance further training in Milan, but the Conservatoire rejected him in 1832. Private study with Vincenzo Lavigna, who had worked at La Scala, gave him access to counterpoint and practical theatrical knowledge instead. In 1836 he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took up municipal musical duties in Busseto. His route to opera passed through a provincial network of patronage, church work and teaching.

The first opera, Oberto, reached La Scala in 1839 and secured further commissions. By then Verdi had lost his daughter Virginia; his son Icilio died that year, and Margherita died in 1840. The comedy Un giorno di regno failed at La Scala in September 1840. Nabucco brought success in March 1842. Temistocle Solera’s libretto offered large public scenes, sharply opposed groups and an exiled people whose collective song could carry a dramatic burden usually assigned to a principal singer.
